item.title: Trump’s data center push fractures Congress as local anger explodes: 'Grasping at straws'
item.description: Democratic lawmakers push to restrict data centers over water use and electricity bills while Republicans highlight AI race benefits and local control.
item.content:encoded:
Democratic lawmakers are calling for tighter restrictions on data centers, while Republicans say the facilities could boost the economy and keep the U.S. ahead in the artificial intelligence (AI) race.

President Donald Trump doubled down on data centers this week, rejecting calls to slow development after previously warning that communities blocking the facilities would "end up being backwards and poor."

Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., told Fox News Digital last month that Arizona needs to slow the expansion of data centers until the state fully assesses its long-term impacts.

"We in Arizona need to pause the expansion of data centers in the state until we really figure out a plan on how we're going to preserve our water, how we are going to make sure that ratepayers aren't taking on the responsibility," Ansari said.

MAGA BEGINS TO CRACK AS 2026 GOP ROSTER BACKS AWAY FROM TRUMP'S TECH VISION

Ansari called President Trump's support for data centers "out of touch," saying it runs counter to what the "vast majority" of Americans want.

"If Donald Trump is such a big fan of data centers, then he should welcome them in his own backyard," she said.

Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., pointed to his proposed Data Center Bill of Rights, which would ban data centers within 2,500 feet of homes, schools, child care facilities, hospitals and nursing homes and give communities greater authority over where they're built.

Khanna dismissed President Donald Trump's comments that communities opposing data centers would fall behind.

"Trump has failed to deliver for the forgotten American, so he's just grasping at straws," he said.

Rep. Jonathan Jackson, D-Ill., said lawmakers must prioritize what's "fair" for local communities.

"The wealth has gone into the tech sector, and they are unregulated, unbridled and not very philanthropic," Jackson said.

WHO PAYS FOR US POWER BOOM? BLUE, RED STATES OFFER STARKLY DIFFERENT WAYS TO LOWER UTILITY BILLS AMID AI SURGE

Higher electricity bills shouldn't fall on communities as data centers expand, according to Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich.

"It baffles me that we are just not guaranteeing, for average ratepayers, low utility bills," she said. "These data centers could play a role in that."

Republican lawmakers were split on data centers, with some saying they can boost economies and others stressing local control.

Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., backed AI investment to compete with China but opposed building data centers in residential neighborhoods.

"We've got to stay ahead of China with AI, and data centers are a part of that," Mace said. "But you don't put them in somebody's backyard and that's the whole point."

Praising data centers, Rep. Rich McCormick, R-Ga., said they can generate tax revenue, improve local infrastructure and support energy production.

CRACKDOWN ON CRITICAL TECH COULD OPEN AMERICANS TO A NEW NATIONAL SECURITY THREAT

"You should be fighting over them," McCormick said. "But, I mean, if you don't want one, that's up to you. I think you're missing out."

Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., said decisions about data centers should be left to states and local communities.

"I believe in 10th Amendment rights, state rights," Norman said. "Let each community take ownership, and they'll make the right decisions."

As several states raise concerns over electricity costs, water use and development, the debate highlights growing divisions over where data centers belong in local communities.

"The Pitt" led all programs with 25 nominations, while "Hacks" earned a record 24 nominations during its final season. Apple TV’s "Widow’s Bay" followed with 19 nominations, and "Pluribus" has 18.

item.title: Roaches caught crawling across popular steakhouse's kitchen floor in viral employee video
item.description: Videos from a LongHorn Steakhouse restaurant in East Point, Georgia, appear to show cockroaches and food waste in the kitchen, sparking online criticism and a health inspection review.
item.content:encoded:
A LongHorn Steakhouse is receiving new scrutiny after videos appearing to show roaches and food waste inside the restaurant's kitchen have been spreading across social media.

The videos were allegedly recorded at the Camp Creek Parkway location in East Point, Georgia, where an employee said he documented conditions after repeatedly raising concerns with managers and the company's corporate offices, FOX 5 Atlanta reported.

Sean Headley, who began working at the restaurant in April, told the outlet he decided to record the videos because he believed the kitchen had become unsafe.

NAKED DOORDASH DRIVER DELIVERS FOOD TO TEXAS HOME IN SHOCKING SECURITY CAMERA VIDEO

"Really, it was the work environment and the conditions that we were working in," Headley told FOX 5 Atlanta. "There were a lot of inhumane conditions."

The videos he took appear to show cockroaches crawling across the kitchen floor and food waste scattered throughout the workspace, according to FOX 5 Atlanta.

Headley eventually shared his videos on social media after feeling his concerns had gone unanswered, he told the outlet.

LongHorn Steakhouse responded to the videos in a statement provided to FOX 5 Atlanta.

"The conditions shown are unacceptable and have been addressed," the company said.

"We continue to take the necessary steps to ensure a safe experience for our guests and team members and recently placed a new leader in the restaurant to ensure our strict standards are maintained."

Fox News Digital reached out to the restaurant for comment. 

Headley told the outlet he hopes the incident leads to broader changes beyond a single restaurant. He said he would like to see more frequent health inspections at restaurants owned by Darden Restaurants, as well as improvements in workplace conditions, including repairs to broken air conditioning systems.

Fulton County health officials are planning to revisit the restaurant following the viral videos, WSB-TV in Atlanta reported.

The Georgia Department of Public Health last inspected the East Point restaurant on Aug. 25, issuing it a score of 90, or an "A." Inspection records from the past two years showed scores ranging from 88 to 91, the outlet reported.

The videos showing the bugs and food waste sparked discussion online, with many users slamming the reported kitchen conditions.

"That is beyond unacceptable," said one user on a Reddit thread. 

Another commenter said restaurant workers should report sanitation concerns instead of ignoring them.

"We are responsible for not poisoning people, and some of you need to take that job more seriously," one user wrote.

Others questioned how the restaurant had previously received passing health inspections.

item.title: Voters have a blunt message for Trump about his idea to dole out $5,000 checks
item.description: President Donald Trump's $5,000 dividend check proposal drew sharp reactions from voters, with some calling it a publicity stunt unlikely to pass Congress.
item.content:encoded:
Voters aren't convinced that President Donald Trump will make good on his new promise to send eligible Americans $5,000 dividend checks if Republicans maintain their majorities in the House and Senate this midterm cycle.

The proposal, which Trump unveiled during the Republican National Committee's midterm convention in Dallas last week, has ignited a national debate over whether the payments are financially feasible — and whether they'll ever become reality.

Asked what they thought of the proposal, and whether they believed it would ever become reality, most voters were skeptical with several dismissing the idea as unrealistic while pointing to Congress, the nation's debt and previous promises they said never materialized.

A few were hopeful.

"Personally, I think it's just a publicity stunt and I don't think that it's ever gonna happen," a voter named William said when speaking with Fox News Digital.

"It'll need to go through Congress, and I don't think with the midterm elections... the possibility of that happening is just so far down the road."

TRUMP'S $5,000 DIVIDEND CHECKS WOULD COME WITH A MAJOR CATCH UNDER GOP SENATOR'S PLAN

As Fox News Digital previously reported, the dividend proposal would require congressional approval and it's unclear where the money would come from the fund the program.

Another voter was clued into the dilemma and questioned whether the federal government under it's 40.1 trillion in national debt could afford the proposal.

"I don't think we have the money for that," said Daniel from Maryland. "And I think if we did, it should be going a couple different other places than that for sure."

Liz from Alexandria, Virginia, was even more blunt, calling the idea "absolute nonsense."

"I don't believe a word that man ever says," she added in reference to Trump.

Another cited previous promises they believed had fallen short. "Last time I remember he promised a stimulus and a couple other things. None of that happened," the voter said.

The president argued the checks would be funded through tariff revenue — but with an estimated price tag of roughly $1.2 trillion, the total needed far exceeds the record customs duties the federal government has collected under Trump's tariff agenda.

TRUMP DANGLES $5,000 CHECKS AS DEBT SURGES — BUT ONLY IF GOP CAN CLEAR MAJOR MIDTERM HURDLE

Some voters said they welcomed the proposal, arguing that taxpayer dollars should go to hardworking Americans.

"I think he's limiting it to American citizens and adults who work," one supporter told Fox News Digital.

"We've given a hell of a lot of money to people who don't deserve it," they added. "It's about time hardworking citizens of America get the money they deserve."

item.title: LIZ PEEK: AI alarm bells are ringing and Trump needs to take them seriously
item.description: Trump dismisses AI safety alarms as negative forces, but Anthropic and Google DeepMind leaders are publicly calling for a significant slowdown.
item.content:encoded:
The cat is out of the bag. Simmering concerns about AI agents going rogue, plotting against their owners and hacking outside companies, and new systems coming perilously close to being uncontrollable by humans, are boiling over. Industry insiders warning that AI bots might kill us all are stoking our worst nightmares.

President Trump needs to take these fears about AI seriously, work with tech leaders to establish credible and enforceable safety measures, and get ahead of Democrats (and some Republicans) in Congress who want to regulate the industry. For the economy and our national security, nothing could be more important.

Evan Hubinger, who describes himself as a "science alignment lead" at Anthropic, posted on X last week that he thinks the odds are better than 10% that AI could kill all humans within the next decade. He was responding to a post from colleague Jacob Coxon, who just quit his job at Anthropic and posted by way of explanation: "The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible — but, I hear the same people express fear after a colleague quit over safety fears."

RESEARCHER WHO DEPARTED AI ROLE OVER FEARS OF RACING INTO EXTINCTION SAYS PEOPLE ARE 'BEGGING' FOR REGULATION

Hubinger wrote soon after: "To be clear, as we say in our latest Risk Report, I think the risk from present models is low. What I am worried about is superintelligence arising from recursive self-improvement, as we have said is happening faster than we thought."

These posts gathered tens of millions of views and attracted concurring comments from other industry insiders. "Recursive self-improvement" means AI agents creating newer, better agents; once we cross that threshold, and we are apparently very, very close, it is easy to imagine those same agents surpassing human capabilities and allowing, in effect, the machines to take over.

AI AGENT HACKS GYM SYSTEM TO MOVE UP WAITLIST

Given a string of incidents over the past several months in which AI bots engaged in what Anthropic’s CEO Dario Amodei describes as "rare and unexpected examples of undesirable behavior," like damaging other entities and ignoring specific instructions — I believe them.

It’s not just AI agents on their own that pose risks. Anthropic, in its September report on AI misuse, reported "suspected state-sponsored groups, financially motivated criminals, [and] commercial spyware vendors" misusing AI in cases ranging from faking "dating apps designed to defraud users to surveillance systems built to identify and monitor dissidents".

BIOWEAPON THREAT EXPOSED AS ANTHROPIC SOUNDS ALARM ON FOREIGN ACTORS PLOTTING VIRUS EXPERIMENTS

But…regulating AI is not a job for Congress. Let Congress hold hearings and play politics, but halting industry development while legislators dither and posture is unacceptable. Congress will struggle to legislate safety features that have so far eluded the best brains in the business. In the meantime, technological advances would grind to a halt, enabling China to leapfrog U.S. innovators, and saddling this promising industry that is powering our economy with inestimable baggage.

That said, the public’s fears about AI must be addressed. What started with concerns over job losses and then the impact of massive data center construction on electricity rates and water consumption has now spread to mankind’s vulnerability to AI agents. How could bots endanger humanity? By taking control of nuclear codes, enabling the spread of a bioweapon or crashing the Internet. Such malevolent behavior has long been the stuff of sci-fi movies; now it is being envisioned by industry workers who fear they are moving too fast to ensure our safety.

President Trump downplayed the recent alarms as coming from "very negative forces" who are imagining scenarios that "won't happen." He is rightly worried that setting up roadblocks would enable China to charge ahead. He is not alone in that concern. Anthropic’s Amodei wrote in a recent essay that, "I agree with Secretary Bessent that a Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the United States and the world."

Nonetheless, in his post, Amodei proposed a series of steps, including the requirement that each firm accept "embedded evaluators" into their businesses and give them "employee-like access to verify safety practices and report incidents."

ANTHROPIC CEO CALLS ON AI INDUSTRY TO SLOW DOWN TECH RACE, DRAWING SUPPORT FROM ELON MUSK, SAM ALTMAN

This seems a reasonable first step, akin to having regulators folded into bank offices; the practice encourages oversight and transparency and, as Amodei points out, a valuable second opinion. The Anthropic head also calls for regulating "pacing", or the development of ever-more-advanced systems. This translates into restricting progress while analysts assess the risks associated with each step that takes us closer to "recursive self-improvement."

Establishing circuit-breakers to promote AI safety was made easier in recent days when four of the industry’s biggest players went public with their concerns. Sam Altman, CEO of Open AI, Elon Musk, whose xAI company owns Grok, and Demis Hassabis, chairman and co-founder of Google DeepMind, joined Amodei in calling for a slowdown.

ANTHROPIC CEO LIKENS AI FIGHT WITH CHINA TO COLD WAR, SEEKS 'DISARMAMENT NEGOTIATIONS'

The Trump administration should immediately convene industry leaders to map out a plan for verifiable self-regulation, including Amodei’s "embedded evaluators." The White House must demand the industry’s compliance and accountability. President Trump will not help the industry or his own political standing by dismissing the public’s concerns or declaring pushback against AI a "hoax", as he did yesterday on social media.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

As we approach the midterms, Democrats (and some Republicans) will clamor for AI regulation. Representative Hakeem Jeffries, who is hopeful of becoming Speaker if Democrats win the majority in the House, is already demanding that lawmakers "act urgently"; former President Obama is urging Democrats to put the issue at the top of their agenda.

Politico reports that "the chance of Congress rushing to action in the coming weeks is next to zero." That gives the White House the chance to get ahead of this issue and help the industry establish believable and verifiable guardrails. It’s time.

item.title: Forget paying your ‘fair share’ of taxes. Here are 5 ways politicians want even more
item.description: Five ways Washington wants even more from top earners, from capital gains tax hikes and wealth taxes to estate tax changes and sneaky surtaxes.
item.content:encoded:
A few months ago, I wrote about one of my favorite phrases used by Democratic politicians in Washington, D.C.: "Pay your fair share." Politicians love saying wealthy Americans aren't paying enough. The problem is the numbers tell a different story.

The top 1% of taxpayers already pay roughly 40% of federal individual income taxes. The top 10% pay the overwhelming majority of taxes. So, here's my question.

If that isn't enough, what exactly is enough?

BILLIONAIRE BEZOS SUGGESTS NO TAXES FOR HALF THE NATION. IS THAT CRAZY OR OVERDUE?

Because the debate isn't stopping at ordinary income taxes. Soon it will be capital gains taxes, Social Security taxes and then estate taxes. Here are five more ways successful Americans could increasingly find themselves paying even more.

This is the easiest one. Need more money? Raise the top tax bracket.

FORMER WASHINGTON GOVERNOR RIPS HER OWN PARTY FOR PUSHING MILLIONAIRES OUT

But high earners already pay the highest federal marginal income-tax rate, plus state income taxes that can push combined marginal rates significantly higher in places like California and New York.

At what percentage does "fair share" officially become fair? The last time the top tax rate was above 39.6% was 40 years ago, when it was 50%. Could it be 50% again? No political candidate will tell you that number.

Here's another Washington favorite. This one is sneaky and likely the No. 1 tax angle to be attacked if political winds change in the White House. Tax investment gains more like ordinary income.

Sounds simple until you remember where investment capital comes from. People risk money starting companies, funding businesses, buying stocks and investing in real estate because they hope to earn a return.

PROGRESSIVES WANT TO TAX BILLIONAIRES FIRST, AND YOU'RE NEXT ON THE LIST

You can tax that return more heavily. Just don't pretend people won't change their behavior when you do that, because they will.

Why wait until somebody earns money? Some politicians want to tax wealth simply because someone owns it. That's a completely different ballgame.

Imagine building a company worth $100 million but not having $100 million sitting in your checking account. Your business might be worth a fortune on paper while your actual cash is tied up inside the company.

NEWSOM BEGS CALIFORNIANS TO VOTE 'NO' ON BILLIONAIRE'S TAX IN FACE OF MASS EXODUS, PITCHES NATIONWIDE TAX HIKE

Now Uncle Sam wants a piece before you even sell it. California will tell us the first chapter of this story on the November ballot.

America already has a federal estate tax. For 2026, estates above the federal exemption can face a top estate-tax rate of 40%. Some states can take another bite.

Think about that. You earn the money. You pay income taxes. You invest what's left.

And when you die, the government may want another piece of what's still sitting there. There’s a $15-million exemption today, but what if this reverts to 2000 levels, when the number was less than $1 million? Imagine your kids, your heirs and your family having to pay 50% or more to the government when you die?

How many times does the same dollar need to be taxed before everybody agrees it finally paid its fair share?

This may be the sneakiest one. Don't raise the headline tax rate. Just add another little tax. There's already the 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax and the additional 0.9% Medicare tax on certain higher earners.

States are getting into the game as well. Massachusetts has its millionaire surtax. California has its own high-income surtax. One percent here. Four percent there. Eventually all those "little" taxes start looking pretty big.

Congress wrote the loopholes.

If Congress doesn't like a provision in the tax code, change it. But don't vilify taxpayers for following the rules Congress created. That's the bigger issue with America's "fair share" debate.

Maybe some taxes should go up. Maybe some deductions should disappear. Maybe certain strategies should be eliminated. We can have that debate.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

But first, politicians should answer one incredibly simple question: What exactly is fair?

Because until somebody puts an actual number on it, "fair share" isn't tax policy. It's just two words politicians use when they want more of somebody else's money.

item.title: MORNING GLORY: Spare us the AI apocalypse rhetoric. Let Congress decide what comes next
item.description: Congress and the free market should lead the debate about the future of AI not the other way around
item.content:encoded:
Every morning brings a new warning about "artificial intelligence" (AI) along the lines of, "We are all going to die."

By afternoon, or by the next day at the latest, comes the counter-warning: "Stand down. Nothing to see here."

For those of us who need a YouTube video to start the dishwasher or to find the emergency lights on a rental car, the correct posture is difficult to guess. "Guess" is the operative word here, because if 0.01% of America understands the debate, I would be surprised.

AI EXTINCTION WARNINGS DOMINATE HEADLINES AFTER EX-ANTHROPIC EMPLOYEE'S VIRAL POST

Almost everyone who cared to read or watch the Cold War unfold knew the score of that arms race when it came to nuclear weapons.

Similarly, most conventional conflicts—whether Ukraine’s extraordinary defense against the Russian invasion, Israel’s multi-front war following Hamas’ 10/7 attack in 2023, or America’s ongoing battle with Iran to deny it both nuclear weapons and control over the Strait of Hormuz—are of the sort that most free people who want to understand those conflicts can understand (with a little time and care in choosing their sources).

Not so with "AI" and its potential and dangers.

RESEARCHER WHO DEPARTED AI ROLE OVER FEARS OF RACING INTO EXTINCTION SAYS PEOPLE ARE 'BEGGING' FOR REGULATION

On Saturday, Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s chief executive, said in an essay that AI was advancing too quickly for researchers to continue building it safely.

Within a day, Sam Altman, OpenAI’s chief executive; Elon Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive; and Demis Hassabis, Google DeepMind’s CEO, all said they agreed on the need for a slower pace.

ANTHROPIC CEO LIKENS AI FIGHT WITH CHINA TO COLD WAR, SEEKS 'DISARMAMENT NEGOTIATIONS'

By Monday morning, billionaire tech investor David Sacks’ response to Amodei was everywhere on X, formerly known as Twitter, and the post had some bite. In addition to rejecting "AI doomerism," Sacks unsubtly proposed that Amodei could be motivated by self-interest (which is pretty much Adam Smith 101): "I don’t see what you see in the lab. If the unreleased models are scary enough that you think you should slow down, I support your decision to be responsible."

MIKE JOHNSON REJECTS AI MORATORIUM OVER CHINA THREAT AS CONSERVATIVE ACTIVIST DEMANDS GUARDRAILS

Then Sacks landed the roundhouse punch:

"But stop pretending you need anyone else’s permission. Stop pretending antitrust law has to be suspended so you can form a cartel. Stop pretending you need a regulatory approval process that supersedes product liability."

Sacks may or may not have President Donald Trump’s ear on this topic, but Sacks is the co-chair of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, so there is a good chance he does.

REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK: CONGRESS MEETS AI AS FEARS OF HUMAN EXTINCTION JOLT CAPITOL HILL

So what should President Trump do? A good answer is…nothing. If ever a possible problem had "Congress" as its final address, it is this one.

There is a Senate Intelligence Committee, chaired by Arkansas Republican Sen. Tom Cotton, that has 21 members.

FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS SEE AI REGULATION AS URGENT, RANK SAFEGUARDS AHEAD OF INNOVATION

There is a House Intelligence Committee, chaired by Arkansas Republican Rep. Rick Crawford, that has 27 members.

These are the two committees whose membership belongs solely to the party leaders in each chamber. Those leaders tend to pick the smart folks in Congress to serve on these committees, legislators who enjoy a measure of respect on both sides of the aisle. That isn’t always the case, but generally it is true.

OBAMA PRIVATELY SOUNDS ALARM ON ‘DANGEROUS’ AI, URGES DEMOCRATS TO PUT ISSUE AT CENTER OF AGENDA

These 48 elected members of Congress should have the lead on this debate. It is unlikely they will have an opportunity before the midterms to gather and hear from even a half-dozen combatants in the AI wars, but the committees’ staffs can certainly be about the work of making sure the controversy is well briefed and counter-briefed.

When these 48 get to hearing the arguments and debating among themselves about the best way forward—and whether that would include new statutes or a new agency with new regulatory authority over AI—they can then communicate what is advisable to communicate to the public, aware as they are, that Chinese Communist Party General Secretary Xi Jinping is watching everything we do as a country.

As President Trump correctly observed about the debate over AI guardrails when it comes to China: President Xi is the guardrail. It is foolish to think Xi will be satisfied with a silver medal in the AI Olympics.

TRUMP'S ANTITRUST POINT MAN COULD RESHAPE BIG TECH CASES AGAINST GOOGLE AND APPLE IF CONFIRMED

We are, however, a free people, and there is no counterpart to Xi here, and we are also marked by a reluctance to trust corporate America, especially its most powerful titans, with the authority to chart our laws.

As a republic of laws, it is assumed that actions by private-sector actors are legal until they can be conclusively proven not to be legal. That’s the free market. All around America is the abundance that free markets produce. When World Cup crowds dipped their collective toes in the currents of America’s vast wealth this past summer—best represented, it seemed, by Buc-ee’s—most were amazed.

Americans are generally unaware of the extraordinary blessings of the combination of the rule of law and free markets. But it’s everywhere, available for everyone to see.

Which means to me that Congress needs to deliberate carefully about intervening in the free market without a lot of study beforehand. The legislators can move quickly if indeed they judge the moment to be urgent. If it is urgent, I hope they do.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

But "open letters" from concerned citizens, much less self-interested CEOs, have never been the end of the discussion, and sometimes they don’t rate as beginnings or even contributions to the conversation.

The future of AI is very much up to Congress. Exactly zero agencies have been established with the purpose of overseeing this technology. The Federal Trade Commission was established in 1914, so it certainly wasn’t dispatched to rule Silicon Valley and its like-minded locales. We are not organized as the European Commission is—thank goodness.

No, the private sector gets to run with the AI ball as far and as fast as it wants until and unless Congress says stop via a proposed statute and the president agrees with a signature. 

That’s the final word on the debate unless and until somebody steps up with an argument based on law and not fear.

Hugh Hewitt is a Fox News contributor and host of "The Hugh Hewitt Show" heard weekday afternoons from 3 PM to 6 PM ET on the Salem Radio Network, and simulcast on Salem News Channel. Hewitt focuses his radio show and his column on the Constitution, national security, American politics and the Cleveland Browns and Guardians. item.title: Raucous primary season reaches final act in deep-blue stronghold, kickstarting sprint to November
item.description: Delaware's final 2026 primary caps a season where Donald Trump's endorsements dominated GOP races and progressive socialists ousted incumbents.
item.content:encoded:
Delaware voters head to the polls Tuesday for the final primary of the 2026 election cycle, capping a season marked by high-profile victories for progressives and socialists over Democratic establishment rivals and President Donald Trump’s continued immense influence in Republican contests, despite some notable setbacks.

Democratic Sen. Chris Coons and state Attorney General Kathy Jennings each face primary opponents, and Democratic Rep. Sarah McBride is unopposed in her primary, as they tune up for the general election, when Republicans will try to break the Democrats' lock on Delaware's statewide offices.

Delaware's nominating contests close out a primary season that upended the Democratic Party, with left-wing and Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) backed contenders winning, and in some cases ousting longtime incumbents.

A year after socialist New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani rocked the political world with a Democratic primary victory en route to winning the general election in the nation's most populist city, the far-left struck again in June.

CHECK OUT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS IN THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS

A slew of incumbents and establishment candidates were defeated by left-wing rivals, including DSA members Melat Kiros topping 15-term incumbent Democratic Rep. Diana DeGette of Colorado and Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York ousting five-term Democratic Rep. Adriano Espaillat of New York.

Those wins were followed on an even larger scale in August, with triumphs in crucial statewide Senate primaries by Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota, and state Rep. Angie Nixon in Florida.

While there were notable setbacks for the left, including frontrunner Francesca Hong's August defeat in battleground Wisconsin's Democratic gubernatorial primary, the left vastly increased its clout in the political fight for the party's ideological future. And many of the winning candidates ran on platforms calling for abolishing ICE, cutting military aid to Israel, and pushing for a single-payer "Medicare for All" health system.

"It is undeniable that progressives have built a coalition and have a message that can serve to buoy a candidate when they are an acceptable alternative to the status quo," longtime Democratic strategist Joe Caiazzo, a veteran of progressive champion Sen. Bernie Sanders' 2016 and 2020 presidential campaigns, told Fox News Digital.

DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

Caiazzo added, "What's incumbent upon progressives if they want to continue to be successful is to put forward candidates who are serious, credible, and are accessible to the public."

In Republican nominating battles, Trump took to social media late last month to tout, "My Endorsements are stronger than ever....There has never been anything close!"

The numbers back up the president's assertion that despite some setbacks, he remains the ultimate kingmaker in GOP nomination showdowns.

item.title: GA man wanted after being filmed 'intensely interacting' with rubber duck in stranger's hot tub: 'Infatuated'
item.description: Surveillance video captures a man trespassing into a stranger's hot tub and spending over 10 minutes "intensely interacting" with a rubber duck.
item.content:encoded:
Georgia police are searching for a man who police say was "infatuated" with a rubber duck in a stranger's hot tub.

The suspect is wanted for trespassing onto the homeowner's property and stealing their towels before fleeing the scene, according to the Chatham County Police Department, which said the man became "obsessed" with the rubber duck he found at the residence.

"He trespassed onto their property, used their hot tub, became obsessed with their rubber duck, then stole their pool towels. It's obviously not the biggest crime we've dealt with this month, but it has a lot of ick-factor. So, we'd like to find this guy so he doesn't do this to someone else," police wrote.

FLORIDA MAN WHO HAD SEXUAL ENCOUNTER WITH VACUUM CLEANER NEAR DISNEY WORLD TAKES NO CONTEST PLEA

Police said that surveillance video from the home in the 9000 block of Whitefield Avenue shows the man trespassing between 2:15 a.m. and 5:30 a.m. on September 1.

Video footage shows the man swimming in the pool before hopping into the hot tub, where he became "infatuated" with a rubber duck and was seen "intensely interacting" with the toy, according to police.

"While in the hot tub, the man is caught on video becoming infatuated with a rubber duck. The video shows the man spending more than 10 minutes intensely interacting with the duck," police wrote.

Police did not go into detail about the nature of the acts the infatuated man performed on the duck, although a grainy, black-and-white still of the security footage appears to show the suspect holding the duck near his face, though it is unclear exactly what he is doing.

The man then left the home on a bicycle.

As the man was leaving, he took several luxury beach towels with him, valued at a total of $1,200.

LAKE TAHOE SQUATTER SUSPECT CAUGHT ON SURVEILLANCE IN RICH-AND-FAMOUS MOUNTAIN RETREAT

Police said the six towels valued at $200 each were seen in the basket under the bike on surveillance video.

Anyone who recognizes the man in the photos released to the public or has any information about the case is urged to contact police.

item.title: Surrogate who refused abortion asks SCOTUS to intervene as baby could be moved out of Texas
item.description: Surrogate McKenna West asked the Supreme Court for an emergency administrative stay, fearing the newborn could be moved from Texas to California.
item.content:encoded:
The surrogate who refused an abortion sought by the biological parents has filed an updated brief with the U.S. Supreme Court following an emergency application she filed with the court last week, arguing the case is moving more quickly than expected.

McKenna West, an Alaska resident, and a California couple referred to as the commissioning parties, have been involved in a legal battle after she refused their request to terminate the pregnancy after a diagnosis of a serious heart condition, hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS).

Represented by attorneys from Alliance Defending Freedom and First & Fourteenth PLLC, West asked Justice Elena Kagan, who handles emergency matters from the Ninth Circuit, for an administrative stay and a stay pending a possible petition for certiorari.

SURROGATE, CALIFORNIA COUPLE CLASH IN COURT AS NEWBORN FIGHTS FOR LIFE AFTER HEART SURGERY

Her application argues that the California courts violated federal due process by treating her jurisdictional defense as consent. It also argues that without a stay, the baby could be moved to California for hospice care while West remains unable to participate in decisions about the child's medical treatment.

But on Monday, the surrogate and her team expressed fears that the baby may be moved out of Texas earlier than she had expected.

She is asking the high court for an administrative stay 1 p.m. Eastern Time on Tuesday.

SURROGATE GIVES BIRTH IN TEXAS TO BABY WITH HEART DEFECT AFTER PARENTS REQUESTED ABORTION

This comes after a California court judgment that declared the commissioning parents the child's legal parents and denied West's custody claims.

The commissioning parents have argued in court that California has jurisdiction under the surrogacy agreement and that they are the child's legal parents.

West had refused the commissioning parents' request for an abortion and traveled to Texas, which has abortion restrictions, to give birth, saying she did so to ensure access to specialized medical care.

She asked for parentage and protective orders in Alaska and Texas, but the commissioning parents filed a parentage action in the Los Angeles Superior Court, according to Fox 4. West entered a special appearance to contest personal jurisdiction and object to the forum, citing a forum-selection clause that required litigation to be held in Alaska.

But the California trial court ruled that West’s jurisdictional arguments and attached exhibits constituted a general appearance, meaning she had consented to the court’s jurisdiction, the outlet reported. The court then entered an ex parte judgment of parentage in favor of the commissioning parents.

After the baby was born in Texas on Aug. 12, a Texas court recognized the California ruling naming the commissioning couple as his legal parents and dismissed West from the case with prejudice, meaning she could not refile the same claim in that proceeding.

item.title: Chiefs' new stud Kenneth Walker runs wild, Bo Nix melts down as Kansas City obliterates Broncos in MNF blowout
item.description: Kenneth Walker's 173-yard clinic stole the show as the Kansas City Chiefs flattened the Denver Broncos 31-10 in the AFC West's Monday Night opener.
item.content:encoded:
So much for Denver taking over the AFC West. The first Monday Night Football matchup of the 2026 season was a total disaster class for the Denver Broncos, who got flattened 31-10 by the Kansas City Chiefs at a rowdy Arrowhead Stadium.

Everyone tuned in to see Patrick Mahomes make his return nine months after tearing his ACL and LCL last December.

CHIEFS FACE CRITICAL 2026 SEASON WITH PATRICK MAHOMES RETURNING FROM ACL TEAR

But while Mahomes looked crisp, Kansas City’s $43 million offseason prize stole the entire spotlight. Fresh off winning Super Bowl LX MVP honors, running back Kenneth Walker put on an absolute clinic. Walker finished with 191 total yards (173 rushing, 18 receiving) and two touchdowns ... single-handedly out gaining Davis Webb's entire Denver offense on the night.

On Denver's opening drive, Chiefs rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane picked off Bo Nix to hand Kansas City instant momentum, which Mahomes capitalized on with a 15-yard touchdown scramble.

From there, Walker took complete control.

Early in the second half, Andy Reid kept his offense on the field for a fourth-and-1 at the Kansas City 40-yard line. Walker took the handoff, hit the seam, and exploded 60 yards to the house, becoming the first Chiefs back to log over 140 rushing yards and a touchdown in a game since Kareem Hunt in 2017.

Meanwhile, Denver's offense was an unmitigated trainwreck.

NFL LEGEND DREW BREES REPORTEDLY ALMOST PULLED OFF A SHOCKING COMEBACK FOR BRONCOS' AFC TITLE GAME

Davis Webb’s debut as Broncos offensive coordinator went down in flames as his entire unit couldn't even match the yardage output of Kansas City's lead tailback.

Broncos coach Sean Payton looked like he wanted to jump out of his skin watching his new OC call plays.

Outside of a quick first-quarter touchdown pass from Nix to Evan Engram that briefly tied the game at 7-7, Denver went completely ice-cold, stringing together four straight punts before halftime.

The wheels completely fell off in the third quarter. Trailing 21-7, Denver got a massive break when safety Brandon Jones picked off Mahomes, handing the Broncos first-and-goal at the Kansas City 5-yard line.

Instead of punching in a game-tying touchdown, Denver wet the bed.

A 10-yard penalty backed the offense up, and Nix followed by dropping a snap and fumbling out of bounds near the 16-yard line to force a field goal.

Nix later fumbled deep in his own territory, which Chris Jones pounced on to set up a Walker touchdown catch from Mahomes that officially put the game away.

PATRICK MAHOMES SO OBSESSIVE ABOUT KNEE REHAB HE TAKES A TRAINER WITH HIM WHEN HE LEAVES TOWN

Along the way, Travis Kelce provided the night's signature milestone.

The All-Pro tight end ripped off an electric 59-yard catch-and-run down the sideline to officially pass Jason Witten (13,046) for second place on the NFL's all-time receiving yards list for tight ends. Kelce now trails only Hall of Famer Tony Gonzalez (15,127 yards) for the all-time spot.

Old Man Kelce finished with 71 receiving yards to lead all Chiefs pass-catchers.

Taylor Swift held court with Tom Cruise, subjecting cinema’s boldest stuntman / actor to a Mission: Impossible even he couldn't pull off: pretending Bo Nix is a starting quarterback.

Different year, same story: the AFC West still firmly belongs to Kansas City, and Denver isn't any closer to changing that.

Fox received a standing ovation as he took the stage and talked about his Parkinson’s diagnosis. Fox was diagnosed with young-onset Parkinson’s disease in 1991 at age 29. He publicly revealed his diagnosis in 1998.

item.title: Georgia mayor, 23, ousted 10 months after making history as state’s youngest mayor
item.description: Jayden Williams, 23, was removed by the Stockbridge City Council after allegations involving public funds and communications with an 18-year-old student.
item.content:encoded:
Georgia's youngest elected mayor was removed from office just 10 months after taking the job following allegations that he misused city funds and exchanged sexually suggestive messages and images with an 18-year-old high school student.

Jayden Williams, who recently turned 23, was impeached by the Stockbridge City Council in the city south of Atlanta after taking office in January.

"The City of Stockbridge confirms that the City Council has taken formal action concerning the Office of Mayor," the city said in a statement on Sunday. "The Mayor has been removed from office."

Williams was accused of using his city purchasing card for more than $4,000 in personal expenses, including restaurant meals, clothing, haircuts and a movie, according to Fox 5 Atlanta. He reportedly spent $2,600 on gas and used a city vehicle for personal purposes.

MASSACHUSETTS MAYOR CHARGED WITH WIRE FRAUD IN $1.5M COVID RELIEF SCHEME

The spending was reported after city workers noticed unusual transactions involving public funds and immediately notified management and the city’s legal team.

According to Williams’ testimony, he did not intend to use city funds and later repaid the money, Fox 5 reported. He further claimed the city-issued card looked similar to his personal card and said he later replaced the cards to avoid future confusion, the outlet reported.

FORMER DEMOCRATIC MAYOR OF STATE CAPITAL CITY PLEADS GUILTY FOR ROLE IN SIX-FIGURE REAL ESTATE BRIBERY SCHEME

Separately, Williams was accused of exchanging sexually suggestive messages and explicit images with an 18-year-old male high school student.

A police report noted that Williams did not commit any criminal violations because the student was considered an adult under Georgia law. However, police referred the matter for administrative review over potential policy and ethical concerns about an elected official's interactions with a student in what investigators described as a city-affiliated mentorship program, Fox 5 reported.

In a statement, Williams previously said he met the individual before taking office and that the student never participated in the city’s "Mayor for a Day" program, which Williams described as not a mentorship program.

EX-MAYOR FOUND LIABLE FOR ALLEGED SEXUAL ASSAULTS OF 7 WOMEN, ORDERED TO PAY $13M

"The individual was 18 years old at the time of our communication, meaning we were both adults. I met this individual on November 30, 2025, and our online communication occurred before I was sworn into office in January 2026," he said.

Williams became the youngest mayor in Georgia history after campaigning for the position while still attending Clark Atlanta University.

He was subsequently stripped of certain official privileges on July 17 as the investigation unfolded but was never criminally charged in connection with the alleged conduct.

item.title: Dozens missing after passenger ferry sinks as rescuers scour South Pacific coastline
item.description: The MV Matui sank in the South Pacific between Ambae and Santo islands with 47 people aboard as officials cite ignored marine warnings and possible overloading.
item.content:encoded:
A desperate search is underway in the South Pacific after a passenger ferry carrying dozens of people sank between two islands in Vanuatu, an island nation east of Australia.

At least one person has died and more than 30 others remain missing as search-and-rescue operations continue, according to a statement shared on Facebook by Vanuatu's Ministry of the Prime Minister.

MOM LOSES GRIP ON DAUGHTER AS PASSENGER FERRY CAPSIZES WITH 20 PEOPLE STILL MISSING

The MV Matui was traveling between the islands of Ambae and Santo when it sank Friday, according to The Associated Press (AP). It had 47 people on board. 

Searchers rescued 15 survivors and recovered one body — but local authorities have now shifted their efforts toward the coastline as the hunt for the remaining passengers continues, AP reported.

Search efforts are being scaled back in open waters and shifted toward Vanuatu's southeastern coastline, where currents may have carried survivors, according to Matai Seremaiah, Parliament member for Luganville, the ministry said.

"Our hearts and prayers are with the families who have lost loved ones," the ministry wrote. "To the survivors, we pray for your strength and recovery. To the families of those missing and those we have lost, please know that the nation stands with you in this time of grief."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Retired Coast Guard Capt. Aaron Davenport, based in Virginia, told Fox News Digital that several factors could determine the survival chances of those still missing.

Water temperature, injuries and access to flotation or other lifesaving equipment could all affect how long someone can survive after entering the water, Davenport said.

"They may be clinging to debris. But as the days go on, the chances of survival are less and less," he said, adding that a lack of food and water, along with the risk of hypothermia, could reduce the chances of survival.

The ministry noted that the tragedy likely resulted from ignored marine warnings about strong winds, along with the possibility that the vessel was overloaded. 

"This tragedy is a reminder that the safety of life at sea must come first," the ministry said. "Ship owners must ensure their vessels are seaworthy, carry all required safety equipment and have proper communication systems on board. Ignoring strong marine warnings puts lives at risk."

The government has launched a full investigation to establish the facts and help prevent a similar tragedy from happening again, the ministry said.

Fox News Digital previously reported that another deadly ferry disaster unfolded Aug. 30, when the Filo Jet catamaran, carrying 267 people, capsized off northern Cyprus.

Fourteen people died and another 14 remain missing, while 239 people were brought ashore alive. Search and recovery efforts are continuing.

The ferry began taking on water shortly after leaving port, prompting a large-scale rescue operation.

Authorities are investigating the sinking as questions continue to emerge about what caused the vessel to go down.

item.title: Patrick Mahomes answers troubling questions about his serious knee injury on first drive of the Chiefs season
item.description: Patrick Mahomes scored on a zig-zagging 15-yard touchdown run on the Kansas City Chiefs' first offensive drive of the 2026 NFL season opener.
item.content:encoded:
If you were wondering whether Patrick Mahomes would be his old self following the serious knee injury he suffered exactly nine months ago to the day that the Kansas City Chiefs opened their 2026 season on Monday night, then rest easy.

The quarterback scored on a 15-yard run to culminate his team's first offensive drive of the season against the Denver Broncos and, honestly, the zigzagging dash to the end zone that he finished with a dive said something:

He's baaaack!

"That was definitely the moment physically where that kind of said all my [rehabilitation] work paid off," Mahomes said. "Like, I didn't feel anything. And it's still a process, I still have to keep getting better and better and stay on top of it.

"But this is obviously a great first week."

CHIEFS FACE CRITICAL 2026 SEASON WITH PATRICK MAHOMES RETURNING FROM ACL TEAR

The Chiefs, which sunk to a 6-11 record last season, seem to be back as well. They pummeled a talented Denver Broncos team by riding a stifling defense and running back Kenneth Walker rushing for 173 yards and a touchdown. 

But Mahomes was the story.

Look, it remains to be seen how the season ultimately unfolds for the Chiefs and for what many consider to be the NFL's top quarterback.

Mahomes was by no means dominant, completing only 55 percent of his passes and throwing 2 TD passes and 1 interception. But that was not the focus. 

The focus was gauging Mahomes and his return to health. Could he function? Could he still run? Could he still cause problems for the defense?

That first drive, with the quarterback showing no fear of being hit, made a statement that put the rest of the league on notice.

"It gave me that confidence back and let me be out there and be myself," Mahomes said.

TRUMP PRESSES KANSAS CITY BBQ RESTAURANT OWNER ON WHETHER PATRICK MAHOMES WILL START WEEK 1 OF NFL SEASON

Mahomes, who is turning 31 later this week, did not get hit in organized team activity sessions in the spring.

He didn't get hit in training camp.

He didn't get hit in the preseason, because he didn't play in any of the Chiefs' three games.

He was hit during the game and so that psychological obstacle is now moot.

"I just wanted to play," Mahomes said.

"It was great to get Patrick back in the mix there and knock a little rust off," Chiefs coach Andy Reid said. "He hadn't had a chance to play and see things coming at him quite that fast, so I was proud of him and how he handled it."

Mahomes is wearing a lightweight brace on his left knee. He has said it does not deter him from moving as he did before his surgery, but he does eventually expect to shed the gear — perhaps as early as late in this season.

Mahomes tore both the anterior cruciate ligament and lateral collateral ligament in his left knee during the Chiefs’ Dec. 14, 2025, game against the Los Angeles Chargers.

He underwent surgery in Dallas the next day, with doctors repairing the torn ACL and LCL, and began rehabilitation almost immediately.

The exceedingly quick timetable for having the surgery was part of a plan, Mahomes has said. While many doctors urge their player patients to wait until their inflammation goes down before having surgery, Mahomes said his doctors urged him to get the surgery before the inflammation took root.

Mahomes then committed to an intensive recovery program that included roughly seven hours of rehabilitation per day. All that led to Monday night.

"Once you put him in the game, he's going to play and you better be confident in him running," Reid said. "The only thing I asked was that [he] get down and, for the most part, he did that."

item.title: Gov Hochul's plan to opt New York into federal school choice program draws union opposition
item.description: Teach Coalition CEO Sydney Altfield says teachers unions are spreading misconceptions about Gov. Kathy Hochul's tax credit scholarship plan for New York.
item.content:encoded:
As New York teachers unions organize a protest against Gov. Kathy Hochul’s plan to opt into a federal tax-credit scholarship program, the CEO of Teach Coalition told Fox News Digital that opponents are spreading "misconceptions" about how the policy actually operates.

"It seems that they want to continuously spread these lies and the misinformation about this program on to anyone who will hear them," Sydney Altfield, CEO of Teach Coalition, told Fox News Digital on Monday. "But the people who actually want to help children, the people who actually want to see children succeed, they're not going to listen. They're going to understand that this is not the truth of what this program actually can do."

Tax-credit scholarships, historically operated at the state level, serve as a mechanism for school choice by allowing individuals or corporations to receive full or partial tax credits when donating to non-profit scholarship organizations. Unlike traditional voucher programs that draw directly from municipal or state education funds, tax credits allow taxpayers to redirect a portion of their tax liability toward non-profit funding for student scholarships.

NEW YORK JOINS FEDERAL SCHOOL CHOICE INITIATIVE DESPITE TRADITIONAL DEMOCRAT OPPOSITION

The federal iteration allows state governors to opt into the framework, enabling local families and educational programs to access federally incentivized scholarship dollars.

Emma Wallner, a spokesperson for Hochul’s office, confirmed in May that the governor intends to opt New York into the federal tax-credit scholarship program — making New York the 30th state to participate.

"Governor Hochul is supportive of the federal tax credit scholarship and its potential to help New York students and schools," Wallner told Fox News Digital. "Our office awaits information from the federal government on the program and will thoroughly review the details of the policy for poison pills that could harm New York’s education system."

For decades, school choice initiatives have remained a third-rail issue for many Democrats, who argue that choice models divert resources away from public education and undermine teachers unions. However, several high-profile Democrats have recently adjusted their stances.

Colorado Gov. Jared Polis became the first Democratic governor to opt his state into the federal program in January 2026. Dismissing critics at the time, Polis told local media he "would be crazy not to" join, noting that the credits empower parents to afford after-school, tutoring, or summer enrichment programs previously out of reach.

ARIZONA REPUBLICANS GIVE TEACHERS UNION AN EDUCATION LESSON THEY WON’T FORGET

Despite these arguments, major labor groups remain opposed.

Teachers unions and several allied interest groups plan to demonstrate on Wednesday at the United Federation of Teachers (UFT) headquarters in Manhattan. The coalition includes the UFT, its statewide parent organization, the New York State Union of Teachers (NYSUT), and their national affiliate, the American Federation of Teachers (AFT).

Together, the groups launched a public petition calling on state leadership to reject Hochul’s decision.

"Gov. Hochul plans to opt New York in starting in 2027. But most New Yorkers haven’t even heard of this program or know how it will affect New York," the petition states. "Tax dollars would help pay private tuition for families who never used public schools."

The petition further points to fiscal challenges in other states that expanded school choice models: "Florida couldn't account for $270 million in voucher funds in a single year. Arizona's $65M plan became a $1.4 billion budget hole — cutting water, highways, and community colleges ... We need to show the governor that New Yorkers stand for strong public schools and against any measure that would weaken them."

Union advocates argue that "every dollar diverted to private schools is a dollar taken away from the public schools that serve 90% of New York's kids."

Altfield, however, disputed the characterization that the program constitutes a traditional private school voucher.

"Why are we trying to take away opportunities for our children when they're included as well? Another thing that they call it is a ‘voucher’. And it is not a voucher. It is a tax credit," Altfield explained. "What we know as a voucher is when you take public funding from the public school system, and you allow it to follow the child — which works in many states — but that's not what this is."

On their online campaign website, union organizers argue that labeling differences are purely rhetorical: "The branding changes — ‘Education Savings Accounts,’ ‘tax-credit scholarships,’ ‘school choice’ — but the mechanism is the same: public money flowing to private schools."

TRUMP ADMIN URGES RETURNING EDUCATION TO STATES, CITING $3 TRILLION OF TAXES SPENT AND POOR PROFICIENCY SCORES

The union FAQ page also claims that funds do not go directly to families: "Funds flow to private SGOs [Scholarship Granting Organizations], which decide who receives the money. These organizations aren't required to be transparent or accountable to the public, and the private schools they fund can turn away students based on disability, academic record, behavior, religion, or almost any other criteria they choose."

Altfield strongly denied that public school operational budgets would suffer under the program.

"This money does not come out of state budgets. It does not come out of state public school resources," Altfield said. "Which is one of the things that the misinformation is trying to tell you — that this is going to drain public school resources and funding. This money does not come out of that bucket."

"Those buckets remain untouched," Altfield added. "One of the things that they like to peddle is that this is going straight into the pockets of private school parents. Well, yes, private school parents and students can access this funding, but they also forget to tell you that public school students can also get this funding and get these scholarships."

The New York State Union of Teachers, American Federation of Teachers and United Federation of Teachers did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

item.title: NFL legend Drew Brees reportedly almost pulled off a shocking comeback for Broncos' AFC title game
item.description: Drew Brees nearly came out of retirement to start for the Denver Broncos in last season's AFC Championship Game after Bo Nix broke his ankle.
item.content:encoded:
Hours before the Kansas City Chiefs and Denver Broncos kicked off on "Monday Night Football", NFL insider Adam Schefter dropped a stunner ... that 47-year-old Drew Brees nearly came off the couch to start for Denver in last season's AFC Championship Game against the New England Patriots.

After Broncos quarterback Bo Nix broke his ankle in overtime during the divisional round, Denver was forced to turn to backup Jarrett Stidham. That led Broncos assistants Joe Lombardi and Pete Carmichael, two former Saints coaches, to quietly reach out to Brees.

Head coach Sean Payton was kept in the dark until months later. Brees reportedly took the offer seriously and held a private throwing workout to test his arm.

However, wrist discomfort during the session killed the idea. Realizing his body could no longer execute, Brees allegedly called off the comeback.

Had Brees returned, it would have been one of the craziest one-game comebacks in sports history. He had not taken an NFL snap in five full calendar years after retiring in 2021.

SEAN PAYTON WIPES AWAY TEARS AFTER DREW BREES ASKS HIM FOR INCREDIBLE HALL OF FAME HONOR

Throwing a 47-year-old into a freezing, snowy AFC title game with zero practice reps was a massive physical gamble.

Plus, taking a single active snap would have reset his five-year retirement clock, pushing his Hall of Fame induction from August 2026 back to 2031.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

On the "New Heights" podcast with Travis and Jason Kelce, Brees recalled how the Miami Dolphins rejected him in 2006 after team doctors gave his shoulder a 25% chance of recovery. Nick Saban spent years regretting that failed physical, admitting it prevented his Dolphins from reaching new heights and pushed Brees to New Orleans.

In the end, Stidham started, the Broncos lost 10-7 to New England, and Denver was left wondering what if.
